issues.risk: Rendering yesterday's health as though it were current is the failure mode this issue exists to prevent, and it is a labelling problem, not a data problem.

issues.title: The two projections are proved to be the same model
non_scope: Asserting equality of rendered markup rather than of the model
issues.objective: Test that the static and runtime representations of the graph are equal once runtime-only fields are removed, so the published site and the running server cannot become alternate realities.
issues.why: Two renderings of one model diverge silently, and the divergence is discovered by a person who trusted the wrong one. A parity test is the only thing that keeps them honest.
issues.current_state: Only one projection exists today, so there is nothing to compare.
issues.desired_state: One test builds both, strips the runtime-only fields and asserts equality, and it fails when either projection grows a field the other does not know about.
acceptance_criteria: The comparison is over the normalised model, not over HTML
Runtime-only fields are removed by an explicit list that the test owns, so adding one to either side without declaring it fails
The test runs in CI on every change
issues.risk: A parity test that strips too much passes trivially. The stripped list is small, explicit and reviewed.

issues.title: Every menu in this repository comes from one derivation
non_scope: Any hand-written menu entry in a template, a script or a data file
Layout coordinates, columns or component trees expressed as data
issues.objective: Derive the desktop navigation, the mobile navigation, the Cockpit sections, the documentation navigation and the landing links from one projection of the graph, with deterministic grouping and ordering.
issues.why: Five menus mean five edits for one new page, and the fifth is the one everybody forgets. Grouping by facts the model already holds gives an order that is stable without anyone maintaining it.
issues.current_state: Navigation and landing content are assembled per surface. The landing page and the Cockpit each know their own entries.
issues.desired_state: One navigation projection feeds every surface, grouping derives from kind, category, scope and availability, and ordering is deterministic.
acceptance_criteria: Every navigation surface reads the same projection, and none holds its own list
Grouping derives from metadata the model already carries, and ordering is deterministic and stable across builds
Adding a capability or a document changes every menu that should show it with no template edit
An entry unavailable in the current environment is not rendered as an active destination
issues.risk: Derived menus can order badly for a reader while being perfectly deterministic. Semantic grouping with alphabetic ordering inside it is the default; an authoritative order is metadata, never a template edit.

issues.title: The overview is what exists, counted rather than claimed
non_scope: A number typed by a human anywhere in the interface
A heading rendered for a kind with no members
issues.objective: Generate the Cockpit overview and its summary numbers from the graph, showing a section only when the repository actually holds that kind of thing.
issues.why: A dashboard with headings for things that do not exist teaches readers to distrust it, and hand-maintained counts are wrong within a week. Both problems disappear when the overview is a query.
issues.current_state: The Cockpit renders pages derived from the registry and the index. Section presence and any counts are decided in code.
issues.desired_state: Sections appear because their kind has members, counts are computed, and a new kind of thing appears without the overview being rewritten.
acceptance_criteria: Sections are present only when the corresponding kind has members
Every number shown is computed from the graph at build or request time
A kind added to the layer appears in the overview with no change to the overview's own code
The counts on the page match the artifact, proved by a test
issues.risk: Counts on a page are the sort of thing the repository's own rule against numbers in prose exists for. They are computed and rendered, never written.

issues.title: The coverage matrix reports evidence, and never a green cell without one
non_scope: A status a contributor can declare without an artifact behind it
Demanding evidence from purely descriptive metadata that has no behaviour to test
issues.objective: Generate a matrix showing, for every capability, whether it is documented, tested, enforced, benchmarked and exposed, where each cell resolves to an artifact or a relation rather than to a claim.
issues.why: This is the view that makes the graph worth building: it turns the question of what is actually finished into something a person can read in one screen. A cell that is green because metadata said so would make it worse than useless.
issues.current_state: Benchmark coverage exists for capabilities. Documentation, tests and enforcement have no coverage view at all.
issues.desired_state: Each cell resolves to a named artifact — a document, a test, a rule, a benchmark case — and an unresolved claim is reported as missing rather than shown as satisfied.
acceptance_criteria: Every filled cell names the artifact that supports it and can be followed to it
A relation that claims evidence but does not resolve is reported as a gap, and the report says which end failed
The policy for what evidence a kind requires is data, not a condition in the renderer, and a descriptive kind is not asked for a behavioural test
The matrix is available in both projections and in machine-readable form
issues.risk: A matrix that is mostly empty on the first run will be read as an indictment rather than a baseline. It is a starting measurement, and saying so is part of shipping it.

issues.title: One detail view, assembled from what a node actually has
non_scope: A separate hardcoded template per kind unless the presentation genuinely differs
A machine-absolute path in any published output
Identity derived from a display title
issues.objective: Render a capability's detail page from its populated sections and its resolved relations, with a stable deep link and a repository-relative reference to where the information came from.
issues.why: The question a detail page has to answer is where this thing actually comes from. A separate hand-written template per kind guarantees that answer is inconsistent, and a link built from a display title breaks the first time somebody improves the wording.
issues.current_state: The Cockpit renders views over the registry. Deep links and source traceability are not part of the model.
issues.desired_state: One assembly renders any node, showing only populated sections, with a stable link and a repository-relative source reference.
acceptance_criteria: Empty sections are absent rather than rendered blank
The deep link is built from the stable identity and survives a title change
Source references are repository-relative and never machine-absolute
The static projection produces compatible links
issues.risk: Traceability that publishes a path from the machine that built the site is a leak. Repository-relative is the only form that ships.

issues.title: Search over the graph, generated, with nothing to run
non_scope: An external search service for a graph of this size
A hand-maintained index or keyword list
issues.objective: Provide one search over identities, titles, descriptions, tags, categories, commands, routes and documents, from a generated index that works in the static build with no service behind it.
issues.why: A repository this size does not need a search service, and adding one would put the published site behind an availability dependency it currently does not have.
issues.current_state: No unified search exists over the layer.
issues.desired_state: One generated index serves both projections, its contents derive from the graph, and it costs nothing to operate.
acceptance_criteria: The index is generated from the graph and covers identities, titles, descriptions, tags, categories, commands, routes and documents
Search works in the static build with no backend
A newly registered capability is findable after generation with no further edit
The index size is measured and counted against the asset budget
issues.risk: A client-side index grows with the repository until it dominates the page weight. Measuring it now is what makes the later decision to page or trim it a measurement rather than a surprise.

issues.title: The relation view reads the graph and holds no data of its own
non_scope: Nodes or edges written into JavaScript
A visualisation library loaded on pages that do not render a graph
A three-dimensional rendering that replaces rather than supplements the accessible information
issues.objective: Render the relation graph interactively from the generated data, with filters, focus, neighbour highlighting and deep links, loaded only where it is used and bounded in cost.
issues.why: The edges are the reason the model exists, and a static list cannot show them. But a visualisation with nodes written into a script is a second inventory in the least maintainable place available.
issues.current_state: The layer's graphs are derived and rendered for the site. There is no interactive relation view over the composed model.
issues.desired_state: One view reads the artifact, filters by the model's own fields, and is not loaded by pages that do not use it.
acceptance_criteria: Every node and edge comes from the generated data
Filters operate on the model's fields — kind, category, source, surface, availability, relation type and the evidence flags
Zoom, pan, selection, neighbour highlighting, a detail panel and deep links all work, and a selected node resolves to its detail view
The library is lazily loaded and absent from pages without a graph
A textual equivalent of the same relations is available for anyone who cannot use the graph
Initialisation cost on this repository's data is measured
issues.risk: Rendering every node at once is slow and unreadable at the same time. The default view is filtered, and expansion is progressive.

issues.title: A surface with no server behind it is not offered as if it had one
non_scope: Any decision made from a hostname, an address or a build flag inside a page
Rendering a dead destination as if it were live
issues.objective: Make the exposure of backend-only surfaces — the API console, live status, runtime reads — follow from availability metadata, and prove both projections behave correctly.
issues.why: The published site has no server. A link to a runtime console on it is a broken promise, and the usual fix is a check on the page's own address, which is a rule hidden where nobody will find it.
issues.current_state: The Swagger shell and the API are served by the running process. The published site has no way to know that.
issues.desired_state: Exposure follows from availability metadata alone, and there is a test for each projection that keeps it that way.
acceptance_criteria: A backend-only surface is offered as usable only where a backend is available, decided from metadata
The static build contains no active link to a runtime-only surface
Where mentioning an unavailable surface is useful, it is shown as unavailable rather than omitted silently or linked
Both cases are tested — the static build and a running server with the API present
issues.risk: This is the check that quietly rots, because a broken link on a published page fails nothing. The test for it has to run on every build.

issues.title: The Cockpit works on a phone and before JavaScript runs
non_scope: Hiding content below a breakpoint instead of adapting it
Requiring JavaScript to discover a documentation link
issues.objective: Make the Cockpit genuinely usable at narrow viewports and keep its core information present in the served HTML, with JavaScript adding filtering, the graph, live state and search rather than being required to read anything.
issues.why: A control plane that only works on a wide screen is unavailable exactly when somebody needs it. And information that only exists after a script runs is invisible to anything that does not run scripts, including the tests that check the links.
issues.current_state: The Cockpit is server-rendered with its own stylesheet, and its behaviour across viewports has not been established for this material.
issues.desired_state: Navigation, cards, tables, details and the graph's textual equivalent are usable from a narrow phone width upward, nothing overflows horizontally, and the core content is in the HTML.
acceptance_criteria: Navigation, content, tables and details are usable at narrow phone widths through to a wide desktop, with no horizontal page overflow at any of them
Touch targets are usable and focus is visible
The markup is semantic, keyboard navigation works, and status is never conveyed by colour alone
Core information is present in the served HTML before enhancement
issues.risk: Mobile behaviour is the requirement most often declared done from a resized desktop window. It is asserted at real viewport widths by a browser check.

issues.title: Live state is an overlay that degrades to nothing
non_scope: A transport invented for the Cockpit alongside one that already exists
A reconnect loop with no bound
issues.objective: Let the running Cockpit overlay live state — health, peers, runtime metrics, deployment status — over the same graph, through the transport the process already has, degrading cleanly where there is none.
issues.why: Live state is what makes a control plane worth opening. It is also what makes a static page lie, so it has to be an overlay that is visibly absent rather than a field that is silently stale.
issues.current_state: The process has a health capability and peers. No surface subscribes to anything.
issues.desired_state: Live values arrive over the existing transport, are visibly distinct from the snapshot, and are absent rather than stale where no backend answers.
acceptance_criteria: Live updates use the process's existing event transport rather than a new one
Live values are visually and structurally distinguishable from snapshot values
The static projection renders the useful equivalent — what the endpoint is, and that the value is available when a server runs — rather than an empty card
Reconnection is bounded and backs off, and a failed connection does not produce a request storm
issues.risk: Live overlays are where credentials leak into browsers. Everything sent to the client is an allowlisted safe field.

issues.title: The surface rules exist as checks, proved by making them fail
non_scope: A rule with no executable check
Requiring documentation or a test from purely descriptive metadata
Duplicating a constraint an existing rule already enforces
issues.objective: State the durable constraints of this architecture as project rules with executable checks: derived surfaces stay synchronised, a public capability is discoverable, a behavioural capability carries verification, a developer-facing capability resolves to documentation, and the two projections stay equal.
issues.why: Everything in this milestone decays the moment a change can land without a check noticing. A rule that exists only as a document is a suggestion wearing a uniform.
issues.current_state: Project rules exist with checks for derived files, projections, hot paths, benchmark coverage and scope. None concerns UI exposure, capability documentation or verification policy.
issues.desired_state: Each rule has a check, each check has a negative test that proves it fires, and CI runs all of them.
acceptance_criteria: A change to an authoritative source that leaves any derived surface stale fails the drift check, and the failure names the source to change
A public or developer-facing capability that is not discoverable through the generated interface fails, unless it declares itself internal
A capability with behaviour carries verification appropriate to its kind, decided by typed policy rather than by one rule for everything
A developer-facing capability resolves to canonical documentation, and the coverage is visible rather than only reported
The static and runtime representations must remain equal after runtime-only fields are removed, enforced by the parity test
Each rule has a negative test that proves the check fires, and CI executes every one
issues.risk: Five new rules can make ordinary contribution feel like litigation. Each policy is typed by capability kind so that a descriptive object is not asked for a behavioural test.

issues.title: One skill runs the whole loop, and is itself in the graph
non_scope: Several thin skills where one is enough
A skill that reimplements what the commands already do rather than sequencing them
issues.objective: Provide a skill that discovers capabilities, validates the graph, reports what is missing documentation, tests, exposure or enforcement, regenerates the projections and reports drift — registered, documented, tested and visible like any other.
issues.why: The loop this milestone creates should be runnable by a worker without knowing which command does which part. And a repository that models skills as data should have its own automation as one of them.
issues.current_state: Skills are a registered kind with a contract. None covers this loop.
issues.desired_state: One skill does the whole loop, follows the existing skill contract, and appears in the graph, the interface and the search like everything else.
acceptance_criteria: The skill sequences the existing commands rather than reimplementing their behaviour
It follows the existing skill contract and needs no special-casing to be registered
It appears in the graph, the interface and the search through the ordinary derivation
It is tested behaviourally, on a repository state where something is genuinely missing
issues.risk: A skill that wraps commands adds a layer that can drift from them. It sequences and reports; it does not decide anything the commands do not.

issues.title: The graph's health is answered by the doctor that already answers everything else
non_scope: A separate diagnostic script or command for the Cockpit
A check that recomputes a verdict another engine already produces
issues.objective: Add the graph's diagnostics to the existing health and doctor surface: the graph builds, identities are unique, relations resolve, projections are synchronised, required documentation and verification are present, and nothing unsafe is exposed.
issues.why: The repository has one place that answers whether what it serves is healthy, and every check there delegates to the engine that decides it. A second diagnostic surface for the graph would be a second opinion.
issues.current_state: The health capability aggregates index diagnostics, benchmark coverage and projection staleness.
issues.desired_state: The graph's verdicts join them, computed rather than asserted, in the same machine-readable and human-readable output.
acceptance_criteria: The checks cover graph validity, identity uniqueness, relation resolution, projection freshness, required documentation and verification presence, and the absence of unsafe metadata
Every number reported is computed, not stated
The output is machine-readable and human-readable in the existing shapes
Each check delegates to the engine that already decides it
issues.risk: Building the whole graph inside a blocking check makes the pre-commit hook slow enough to be bypassed, which the performance doctrine already refuses. Its cost is measured against that budget.

issues.title: A browser proves the interface, at the widths people use
non_scope: Pixel comparison of a rendered graph
Selectors coupled to presentational class names
issues.objective: Extend the existing browser checking to cover navigation on desktop and mobile, search and filtering, the detail view, graph initialisation, conditional runtime exposure, link integrity and console errors.
issues.why: Everything in this milestone is finally judged by whether a person can open it. Server-side tests cannot see an overflowing table, a menu that does not open or a script that throws on load.
issues.current_state: A probe script drives the Cockpit's routes and interactions in a real browser.
issues.desired_state: The probe covers the derived surfaces at representative viewports, uses stable selectors and runs in CI.
acceptance_criteria: Desktop and mobile navigation, search and filtering, the detail view and graph initialisation are all exercised
Representative viewports from a narrow phone to a wide desktop are asserted, including the absence of horizontal overflow
The runtime-only surfaces appear when a backend is present and are not offered when it is not
Internal links resolve and the console is free of errors
Selectors are stable identifiers rather than presentational classes
issues.risk: Browser tests are the flakiest thing in any suite. Bounded waits on stable selectors, and no sleeps.

issues.title: Drift in any derived surface fails the build
non_scope: A separate drift script for the new artifacts
issues.objective: Extend the generation check to cover every artifact this milestone introduces — the graph, the static projection, the navigation, the indexes, the search data — so a stale committed projection cannot merge.
issues.why: Generation without a check is a suggestion. This is the mechanism that makes every derived surface in this milestone actually derived.
issues.current_state: The generation check covers the existing target set.
issues.desired_state: The new artifacts are in the same set, and a drift failure names the source to change rather than the file that differs.
acceptance_criteria: Every new artifact is part of the canonical target set and its check
A drift failure names the authoritative source to change, not only the generated file that differs
Generation is deterministic, so an unchanged repository never reports drift
CI executes the check on every change
issues.risk: A non-deterministic generator turns this check into noise within a day, and the response to noise is to disable the check.

issues.title: Nothing private reaches a published page
non_scope: Printing any secret value while scanning
A general secret scanner competing with the repository's existing tooling
issues.objective: Scan the published graph, the static site and everything the client receives for credential material, private environment values and machine-absolute paths, and fail on a finding without printing it.
issues.why: This milestone publishes a description of everything the repository knows. That is exactly the artifact in which an accidental token or a developer's home directory would travel furthest.
issues.current_state: No such scan exists for the site or the Cockpit data.
issues.desired_state: One check inspects the generated data and the built site, reports findings by location and kind, and runs in CI.
acceptance_criteria: Known credential variable names, credential-shaped values, raw authorization material and machine-absolute paths are all detected
A finding names the location and the kind and never the value
A negative test plants a synthetic marker and proves the check finds it
The check runs in CI on every change
issues.risk: A scan tuned to be quiet finds nothing forever. The synthetic marker is what keeps it honest.

issues.title: The interface has a weight, and it is measured
non_scope: A new benchmark system beside the one that exists
A threshold so tight that ordinary content growth fails the build
issues.objective: Measure the generated data, the served HTML, the initial scripts and styles and the graph's initialisation, and hold them to budgets through the benchmark infrastructure the repository already has.
issues.why: A derived interface grows with the repository by construction. Without a measured budget it becomes slow gradually, which is the way that never gets noticed.
issues.current_state: The benchmark infrastructure records distributions per command against a committed baseline. Nothing measures a page or an asset.
issues.desired_state: The interface's weight and initialisation are baselines like the commands', with thresholds that catch a real regression and ignore a byte.
acceptance_criteria: The generated data size, the served HTML size, the initial script and style weight and the graph initialisation are all measured
The baselines live where the benchmark infrastructure already keeps them, with the environment recorded
Thresholds catch a material regression and tolerate ordinary growth, and the policy states which is which
Heavy libraries are absent from pages that do not use them, proved by measurement rather than by intent
issues.risk: Asset budgets provoke arguments about kilobytes. The threshold is set where it detects a category change, not a content edit.

issues.title: The federated model and its two projections are an architecture decision
non_scope: Restating ADR 12 or ADR 13
An ADR that documents the implementation instead of the decision
issues.objective: Record the decision to compose the authoritative registries into one typed graph and to render it as two projections, with the alternatives that were real and the consequences that follow.
issues.why: The choices here — composing rather than centralising, generating rather than fetching, progressive enhancement rather than a client application, availability as metadata rather than a condition in a page — will each look arbitrary to somebody later. ADR 12 decided the Cockpit is a projection; this decides what it is a projection of.
issues.current_state: ADR 12 establishes the Cockpit as a projection of the registry. ADR 13 establishes that web surfaces are discovered from their producers. Neither covers the composed graph or the static projection.
issues.desired_state: One record states the decision, extends rather than restates the two it follows, and says what would have to change to revisit it.
acceptance_criteria: The record follows the repository's ADR format and frontmatter exactly and relates to the decisions it extends
It states the federated composition, the dual projection, progressive enhancement, availability as metadata and the conditional exposure of runtime surfaces
The alternatives — one central manifest, a client-side application fetching the API, a separate site generator — are recorded with why they were not taken
The consequences state what a new subsystem must do to appear, and what it costs when it does not

evidence.command: bin/majordomus adr check; bin/majordomus doctor; bin/majordomus context validate; bash test/run.sh 99_adr
evidence.result: adr-0018 written at .ai/repo/adrs/0020-the-capability-graph-is-composed-not-centralised-and-projecte.md: adr check accepts the whole set with every identity unique and every reference resolving, doctor reports no failure, context validate reports no problem, and the ADR behavioural case passes

issues.risk: Written last, it becomes a summary of the code. It is written when the choice between composing and centralising is still open.

issues.title: The architecture explains itself, from inside itself
non_scope: Duplicating the ADR's reasoning in prose
Repeating full instructions in every directory document instead of composing them
issues.objective: Document the graph, its sources, its relation model, its two projections and the contributor workflow, and let the interface say how it was generated and from what.
issues.why: The whole promise is that a contributor registers a capability in one place and everything follows. That promise is only usable if the one place is written down, and the interface itself is the most reliable location for its own provenance.
issues.current_state: The Cockpit has a document. The composed graph, the relation model and the contributor workflow have none.
issues.desired_state: One architecture document, reachable from the places a reader starts, and an interface that states its own mode, sources and revision.
acceptance_criteria: The document explains the sources, the relation model, both projections, the conditional exposure of runtime surfaces, how a new capability appears without an edit, the rules, the skill and how to debug a missing node
The interface states its own mode, its sources, its schema version and its build revision from safe metadata
It is reachable from the root document, the architecture documents and the interface itself, through existing cross-linking rather than a hand-written list
Any new directory this milestone creates carries its context document per the directory contract
issues.risk: A document explaining a derivation goes stale faster than the derivation. Every value it states about the current repository is generated rather than typed.

issues.title: A synthetic capability proves the architecture instead of describing it
non_scope: Leaving the synthetic fixture in the repository as if it were a real capability
Special-casing the fixture anywhere in the implementation
issues.objective: Register a synthetic capability at its authoritative source alone, and prove it reaches the graph, the interface, the search, the navigation and the static projection with no other edit — and that omitting its required evidence fails enforcement.
issues.why: Every claim in this milestone reduces to one: adding something requires no edit to any surface. That is either demonstrable or it is marketing, and the demonstration is cheap.
issues.current_state: Nothing proves the loop end to end.
issues.desired_state: One test registers a synthetic capability, generates, and asserts its appearance everywhere it should appear — and asserts the failure when its required evidence is missing.
acceptance_criteria: The capability is registered only at its authoritative source, and no surface is edited
After generation it appears in the graph, the interface, the search, the navigation and the static projection
Omitting its required documentation or verification fails enforcement with a message naming what is missing
Supplying the evidence makes every check pass
The fixture is removed afterwards, or kept only where test fixtures belong
issues.risk: A fixture that the implementation learns to recognise proves nothing. It has to be ordinary in every respect.

issues.title: The inventories this replaces are removed, not left running beside it
non_scope: Deleting a list that is genuinely authoritative for something the graph does not model
Leaving a hand-written list in place as a fallback
issues.objective: Find the hand-maintained inventories this architecture replaces — menus, landing cards, route lists, documentation indexes, rule and skill catalogues — and remove them, so that one derivation is the only one.
issues.why: Two systems doing the same job is worse than either alone: the old one keeps working just well enough that nobody notices it has diverged. Migration is finished when the thing it replaced is gone.
issues.current_state: Several surfaces assemble their own lists. Which ones exactly is a reconnaissance result, not an assumption.
issues.desired_state: Each replaced inventory is deleted, its consumers read the derivation, and nothing hand-written survives as a fallback.
acceptance_criteria: The inventories that are replaced are enumerated from the repository, not assumed, and each is either removed or justified as authoritative for something else
Every consumer reads the derivation after the removal
Nothing that was removed is reachable as a fallback path
The built site and the running interface show the same content as before the removal, except where the derivation is more complete
issues.risk: Removing a list that quietly held something the graph does not model loses content. Each removal is checked against what the derivation actually produces.

issues.title: The gate refuses what would silently break the interface
non_scope: A separate workflow for the interface checks
A gate slow enough that people work around it
issues.objective: Put the drift check, the enforcement rules, the parity test, the browser checks and the public-data scan into the existing verification workflow, so that a change leaving any derived surface stale or unsafe cannot merge.
issues.why: Every mechanism in this milestone depends on failing loudly at merge time. Without the gate they are conventions, and conventions are the thing this repository builds machinery to avoid needing.
issues.current_state: The verification workflow runs the repository's existing checks.
issues.desired_state: The new checks belong to the same gate, run on every pull request, and the gate stays fast enough to be usable.
acceptance_criteria: A stale derived surface, a missing required document, a missing required verification, a broken static link to a runtime-only surface and unsafe published metadata each fail the gate
The browser checks and the parity test run on every pull request
Caching keeps the added time proportionate, and the total is measured
No check added here lives outside the existing verification hierarchy
issues.risk: Browser checks in CI are where a suite becomes unreliable. They run against a built artifact with bounded waits, or they do not run at all.

issues.title: The milestone is accepted on its evidence
non_scope: Reporting a derived surface as proved without the artifact that proves it
issues.objective: Close the milestone: every acceptance criterion carries evidence, the measurements are recorded with their environment, the contributor workflow runs as written, and the remaining gaps are stated.
issues.why: A milestone is accepted by its evidence. What a later reader has is the record, not this session.
issues.current_state: Open.
issues.desired_state: Accepted with evidence against every criterion, with the coverage baseline and the limitations written where they will be found.
acceptance_criteria: Every acceptance criterion of the milestone has evidence recorded against it
The coverage matrix baseline is recorded as a starting measurement rather than presented as a verdict
The contributor workflow runs exactly as documented on a clean checkout
Pre-existing failures, failures introduced here and failures fixed here are distinguished explicitly
Remaining limitations are stated rather than omitted
issues.risk: The end of a large milestone is where intent gets recorded as outcome. Anything not demonstrated is written as a limitation.

issues.title: A served surface says which checkout it is serving
non_scope: Publishing an absolute developer path to anything but a loopback surface
A second identity beside the one the repository model already holds
Changing what any surface serves; this changes only what it says about itself
issues.objective: Make every surface a process serves name the repository it is serving — its root and its identity — so that a reader can tell at a glance whether the answers in front of them come from the tree they are working in.
issues.why: This cost a real hour. A browser held a Swagger page from a server that had exited, its requests failed with a message blaming CORS, and the live server on another port turned out to be serving a scratchpad worktree of a different session entirely — so even the document being read was that other tree's, including a sentence about the routes that this tree had already corrected. Nothing on the page said which checkout answered it. Several sessions share one machine and each may bind its own server; a surface that does not name its tree invites exactly this conclusion, that the tool is broken, when the tool is fine and the address is wrong.
issues.current_state: The home page lists the surfaces, the version and a repository identifier, and `/api/v1/repository` will name the root if asked. The Swagger shell and the served document name neither. A stale page fails with a transport error that names CORS before it names a closed socket.
issues.desired_state: Every served surface carries the repository root and identity it is answering for, close enough to the content that a reader sees it without asking for it.
acceptance_criteria: The home page names the repository root and identity the process is serving, not only the surfaces it exposes
The interactive API shell names the same root, so a page fetched from one server cannot be mistaken for another's
The identity comes from the repository model rather than from a second inspection
No surface names the repository's location on the host: the identity says which checkout answered, never where it sits, and a test proves no served or published output carries an absolute path
The behaviour is exercised by a test that serves two roots and proves each surface names its own
issues.risk: The obvious fix — printing the root — is the one to refuse: it would leak the host's directory layout to whoever can reach the socket, and the incident is solved by saying which checkout answered, not where it lives.

issues.title: What this tool leaves behind, established by inspection rather than by memory
non_scope: Moving anything; this issue changes no path
A rewrite of a subsystem discovered along the way
issues.objective: Establish, from the repository rather than from recollection, every path Majordomus writes, generates or mutates when a project adopts it — where each lands, which subsystem writes it, whether anything records it, and which are canonical, derived or accidental.
issues.why: The two-folder contract is a claim about a footprint nobody has measured. Every later phase — the layout, the reconciler, the ledger, the migration — is a decision about paths, and a decision about paths made from memory will be wrong in the way that only shows up in a foreign repository.
issues.current_state: `.ai/` and `.majordomus/` both exist. Provider bootstraps are generated to the root, root documents carry generated blocks, and no inventory says what else a subsystem writes or under what circumstances.
issues.desired_state: One document records the actual footprint with its writer, its lifecycle and its justification, and names which of them the target architecture keeps, moves or removes.
acceptance_criteria: Every path written or mutated outside `.ai/` and `.majordomus/` is listed with the code that writes it, found by inspection rather than by assumption
Each is classified as canonical, derived, generated, cache, runtime or accidental, with the reason
The classification says which paths the two-folder contract keeps as bridges, which move into a namespace and which stop existing
Where an existing mechanism already does what a later phase would add, it is named so the phase extends it rather than replacing it
The architectural decision is recorded in the repository's own ADR mechanism, not in prose beside it
issues.risk: A forensic phase can become a rewrite the moment it finds something ugly. It records; the phases that follow change.

issues.title: The two namespaces are a typed contract, not a habit
non_scope: A configuration file restating what a convention already fixes
Moving existing content; that is the migration issue
issues.objective: Declare the canonical layout of `.ai/` and `.majordomus/` as typed, versioned data — what each namespace holds, what it must never hold, and which lifecycle each directory's contents carry — so that the boundary can be checked rather than remembered.
issues.why: The boundary between portable knowledge and control-plane mechanics is the whole architecture. Stated only in prose it survives until the first subsystem finds it convenient to write an index next to a rule.
issues.current_state: Both namespaces exist and are populated. Nothing declares what belongs in which, and nothing refuses a control-plane artifact written under `.ai/` or a copy of authored knowledge written under `.majordomus/`.
issues.desired_state: The layout is a schema-backed declaration; a check reads it and refuses a path that contradicts it.
acceptance_criteria: Each namespace declares what it holds, in typed and versioned form, generated from the canonical Rust types where generation is available
`.ai/` is defined as portable semantic material that keeps its meaning without this tool and across providers, and `.majordomus/` as control-plane state that must never hold a second copy of it
A check refuses an artifact placed in the namespace whose contract excludes it, and names both the path and the contract it violates
The skeleton a new repository receives is derived from the same declaration rather than being a parallel copy of it
issues.risk: A layout schema can become a second description of the tree it describes. It declares intent and lifecycle; the tree remains what discovery finds.

issues.title: Whether a file is authored or derived is a field, not a naming convention
non_scope: Replacing the existing banner mechanism where it already answers the question
A provenance field that repeats what the schema id already fixes
issues.objective: Give every machine-processable artifact an explicit provenance and lifecycle — authored, derived, generated, cache or runtime — with its generator, its inputs and whether it is disposable, so that no consumer has to infer from a path what a file is.
issues.why: A generated file that is indistinguishable from an authored one eventually becomes an input, and then it cannot be regenerated without losing something. Deciding that by directory name works until the first exception.
issues.current_state: Generated artifacts carry a banner or an extension member saying they are generated, which the manifest validator reads. Nothing states a generator's inputs or whether an artifact may be deleted and rebuilt.
issues.desired_state: Provenance and lifecycle are typed fields every artifact carries, and a consumer decides what it may do with a file by reading them.
acceptance_criteria: Every generated artifact declares its generator, its version and the canonical inputs it derives from
Disposability is explicit, so a consumer can tell what may be deleted and rebuilt from what may not
A generated artifact is never read back as canonical input, and a check proves it
Authored artifacts are distinguishable from derived ones without consulting a path
issues.risk: Recording inputs invites recording them by hand. The input list is derived from the generator, or it is not recorded.

issues.title: Both namespaces carry their contracts, all the way down
non_scope: A second contract format for the second namespace
Duplicating a parent's instructions in every child
issues.objective: Extend the directory-contract discipline that already governs `.ai/` to `.majordomus/`, so every directory of either namespace explains its purpose, its ownership, its lifecycle, the schemas that apply and how its contents are discovered.
issues.why: A control-plane directory nobody documented is where the next copy of something appears. The mechanism for preventing that already exists on one side of the boundary and simply does not run on the other.
issues.current_state: ADR 0011 established that every directory of the layer carries a contract, and a validator enforces it under `.ai/`. `.majordomus/` has no such requirement.
issues.desired_state: The same validator covers both namespaces, and the effective context for an artifact composes from the contracts above it in either.
acceptance_criteria: Every directory of both namespaces carries a contract with valid typed front matter, and a missing one fails the existing validator
Each states purpose, ownership and lifecycle, the schemas that apply, and how its contents are discovered and extended
Contracts compose rather than repeat: a child adds to its ancestors and never restates them
The same mechanism serves both namespaces, with no second format
issues.risk: Mechanical coverage produces mechanical documents. A contract that says nothing a reader could not guess is a cost with no benefit, and the review has to say so.

issues.title: The repository is discovered once, into one model
non_scope: A second index beside the one that exists; this composes it
Discovery that reaches the network or builds anything
issues.objective: Build the one typed model of a repository — identity, structure, capabilities, the layer's registries, workflows, environments, providers, services and version-control state — discovered once and read by every consumer.
issues.why: The CLI, the environment entry, the documentation and the server each discover the repository their own way today, which is four answers to one question and four places to fix when it is wrong. One model is the spine the rest of this milestone hangs from.
issues.current_state: An index of the layer exists and a capability registry exists. Repository facts beyond them — the environment, the providers, the workspace, the services — are read where they are needed, each time.
issues.desired_state: One discovery produces one typed value; consumers hold it rather than the filesystem.
acceptance_criteria: One typed value carries what a consumer needs to know about a repository, composed from the registries that already own their parts
Discovery happens once per process, and a second consumer pays nothing for it
Nothing in the model requires a configuration file to state what inspection can establish
No consumer reads the filesystem for a fact the model already carries, proved by a check rather than by review
issues.risk: A model that knows everything is discovered slowly, and the environment entry pays that cost on every directory change. Its cost is measured in the same issue that makes it mandatory, not later.

issues.title: The registries are views of the model, not separate discoveries
non_scope: A registry file that enumerates what discovery finds
Changing what any kind means; this changes where it is read from
issues.objective: Make the typed registries — skills, rules, decisions, workflows, use cases, providers, capabilities — views over the one repository model, so that adding a valid artifact under a discoverable namespace registers it everywhere with no second edit.
issues.why: Registration by hand is the defect this repository has removed once per subsystem. Doing it once over one model is what stops the next subsystem from reinventing it.
issues.current_state: Kinds are discovered by source classes and indexed; capabilities are declared and projected. The two are joined only in the composed graph, and other consumers still enumerate.
issues.desired_state: Every registry is a projection of the model, and a new artifact appears in the CLI, the API, MCP, the Cockpit, the documentation and search without anything being listed.
acceptance_criteria: Each registry is derived from the model, and no consumer builds its own
Adding a schema-valid artifact under a discoverable namespace exposes it to every applicable consumer with no further registration, proved by a synthetic artifact in a test
A malformed artifact fails loudly with its path and its schema violation rather than vanishing from a listing
Ordering is deterministic, so two runs over one tree produce one answer
issues.risk: Silent omission is the failure mode: an artifact that fails validation and simply does not appear is indistinguishable from one nobody wrote. It has to fail, not disappear.

issues.title: Discovery is deterministic, cached, and its cost is known
non_scope: A cache that can serve a stale answer for a changed input
A persistent cache shared between repositories
issues.objective: Make one discovery over one tree produce one answer, cache it by what it was derived from, and measure what it costs — because everything downstream now pays that cost.
issues.why: A model every consumer reads is on the hot path of every command, including the ones that run when a person changes directory. An unmeasured spine becomes the reason the tool is avoided.
issues.current_state: The layer's flattening is cached by content hash and the executable's phases are timed. The composed model's own cost has not been measured.
issues.desired_state: The cost is a benchmark with a baseline, the cache is keyed by the inputs, and a stale entry cannot be read for a changed tree.
acceptance_criteria: Two discoveries over an unchanged tree produce structurally identical models, with no dependence on directory iteration order
The cache is keyed by the content it was derived from, so a stale entry costs a miss and never a wrong answer
Cold and warm discovery are benchmarked separately with a recorded baseline
A cache hit and a cache miss produce byte-identical output for every read-only command
issues.risk: A cache is a second thing that can be believed. Keying it by content hash means a wrong key costs time, never correctness.

issues.title: The desired integration is a value, and the plan is a diff
non_scope: Applying anything the dry run did not show
A desired state that depends on a configuration file rather than on the model
issues.objective: Compute what a repository's Majordomus integration should look like as a typed value, diff it against what the repository actually holds, and make the apply the smallest mutation that closes the gap.
issues.why: `init` that writes what it was written to write cannot be run twice, cannot be previewed, and cannot be undone. A desired state that is a value can be compared, shown before it is applied, and reversed.
issues.current_state: Initialisation writes a skeleton. Nothing computes what is missing, nothing reports what would change, and running it again is not a defined operation.
issues.desired_state: One function produces the desired integration from the repository model, one produces the difference, and the apply consumes the difference — so a dry run is the same computation without the last step.
acceptance_criteria: The desired integration is derived from the repository model, and a repository that already conforms produces an empty difference
The difference is a typed value that names every path it would create, modify or remove, and why
A dry run performs the same computation as an apply and mutates nothing
The apply performs exactly the difference and nothing else, proved by comparing the tree before and after against the plan
A mutation the plan did not name is a bug, and a test proves the apply cannot make one
issues.risk: A reconciler that computes what a repository should look like will eventually be wrong about one. Everything it would do outside the two namespaces must be visible before it is done.

issues.title: Everything placed outside the two namespaces is recorded, with what it was
non_scope: Recording anything inside the two namespaces, which are owned by construction
A ledger a person is expected to edit
issues.objective: Record every mutation Majordomus makes outside `.ai/` and `.majordomus/` in a typed ledger: the path, the kind of mutation, the content hash as written, the generator and version that wrote it, and what was there before.
issues.why: Without a ledger the tool cannot tell its own edits from a person's, which means it can neither update them safely nor remove them at all. The ledger is what makes an uninstall possible and an overwrite refusable.
issues.current_state: Root documents carry generated blocks and provider bootstraps are written to the root. Nothing records that Majordomus put them there.
issues.desired_state: The ledger is the authority on what Majordomus owns outside its namespaces, and a mismatch between what it recorded and what is on disk stops a mutation rather than resolving it.
acceptance_criteria: Every mutation outside the two namespaces is recorded with its path, its kind, the hash as written, the generator and version, and the prior state
A managed region records the markers that bound it, so the rest of the file is never in question
The ledger is typed and schema-backed, generated from the canonical type rather than hand-written
A path whose current hash does not match what the ledger recorded is reported as edited by a person, and no mutation proceeds on it silently
The ledger contains no secret and no absolute developer path
issues.risk: A ledger that drifts from the filesystem authorises deletions it cannot justify. The hash is what keeps it honest, and a mismatch has to stop the operation rather than warn about it.

issues.title: The second run changes nothing, and a test says so
non_scope: Achieving stillness by making the second run skip work it should do
Ignoring a difference because it is only in a generated file
issues.objective: Make reconciliation idempotent: running it against a conforming repository produces no change at all, and prove it with a test rather than with an observation.
issues.why: Idempotence is what separates a reconciler from a script that happens to run twice. It is also the cheapest possible regression test for the whole desired-state machinery: if the second run does something, the first one did something it could not describe.
issues.current_state: Initialisation is not idempotent and nothing measures whether it is.
issues.desired_state: A second reconciliation reports zero changes, the working tree is byte-identical, and a test fails the moment that stops being true.
acceptance_criteria: Reconciling a conforming repository twice leaves the tree byte-identical, including every generated artifact
The second run reports no change rather than reporting changes it then does not make
The test covers a repository that was already adopted, one adopted by an older version, and one where a person edited a bridge
A deliberate divergence makes the test fail, proving it can
issues.risk: The easy way to pass this test is to make the second run do nothing on principle. The test has to distinguish a reconciler that found nothing to do from one that did not look.

issues.title: Uninstall gives back exactly what was taken
non_scope: Removing authored content under any default
A broad recursive delete of any path not named by the ledger
issues.objective: Implement removal that reverses every recorded mutation, refuses anything a person has since edited, and leaves authored knowledge in place unless removal is asked for separately and explicitly.
issues.why: A tool that cannot be removed is a tool people hesitate to adopt. And the half of the footprint that matters most — the decisions, the handovers, the knowledge accumulated over months — is the project's property, not the tool's leftovers.
issues.current_state: Nothing removes an adoption. What Majordomus wrote outside its namespaces can only be found by reading a diff.
issues.desired_state: One command reverses the ledger, one flag additionally removes generated state, and removing authored content is a separate decision the default never makes.
acceptance_criteria: Every recorded mutation outside the two namespaces is reversed to the state the ledger recorded as prior
A managed region is removed without disturbing the rest of its file, and a file that exists only because Majordomus created it is removed whole
A bridge whose hash no longer matches is left in place and reported, never overwritten or deleted
The default leaves authored `.ai/` content untouched; removing generated state and removing authored content are separate, explicit requests
After the default removal, the repository is what it was before adoption apart from authored content, proved by comparing against a recorded starting state
issues.risk: This is the operation where a mistake destroys somebody's work. Every deletion is justified by a ledger entry and a matching hash, or it does not happen.

issues.title: What touches the root is two small blocks, and they never change again
non_scope: Repository-domain logic in any root file
A bridge whose content depends on the version of the tool that wrote it
issues.objective: Reduce every root-level integration to a small, stable, machine-owned bridge: a managed block in the agent document that points at the layer, and — when direnv is wanted — one line that sources the environment integration.
issues.why: Root files are where an integration becomes visible and where it becomes a nuisance. A bridge that carries no logic never has to change, which means an upgrade touches nothing a person has to re-approve.
issues.current_state: Root documents carry generated blocks whose content is regenerated as the layer changes, and provider bootstraps are written to the root.
issues.desired_state: A bridge names where the truth lives and stops. Upgrading Majordomus does not rewrite it, because there is nothing version-dependent inside it.
acceptance_criteria: Each bridge is bounded by markers, recorded in the ledger, and carries no logic — only a reference to where the canonical material lives
Upgrading the tool leaves the bridges byte-identical, proved by reconciling with a newer version against an older adoption
A bridge is created only when the surface genuinely requires a root file; where a tool can be configured programmatically, nothing is written
The environment bridge is one stable line whose target lives under `.majordomus/`
issues.risk: Every provider that wants a root file argues that its file is special. The answer is the same one: the file is an adapter, and its content is derived.

issues.title: Entering a directory is local, bounded and silent about the network
non_scope: Any network call, any build, any repository mutation on the entry path
A banner that recomputes what a cache already holds
issues.objective: Keep environment entry — the direnv hook, the banner, the shell integration — local, bounded and free of build and network work, and measure it against a declared budget.
issues.why: This runs every time a person changes directory. A second of it is a tax on every action of the day, and a network call in it turns a flaky connection into a broken shell.
issues.current_state: The environment integration exists and its shape is described in the supplied reference. Its cost under the new model is unmeasured.
issues.desired_state: The entry path reads cached, local state, its cost is benchmarked against a stated budget, and a regression fails a check rather than being noticed.
acceptance_criteria: The entry path performs no network request, no build and no mutation of a tracked file
Its cost is measured against a declared budget, cold and warm, and a regression fails the check
What it displays is derived from the same model every other consumer reads, not from a parallel inspection
A repository that has not been adopted produces no error and no noise
issues.risk: Cheap on this machine is not cheap on a cold cache over a network filesystem. The budget is measured on a cold cache, and the environment it was measured on is recorded with it.

issues.title: A provider is an adapter over the model, and adding one is an implementation
non_scope: Provider semantics in the canonical layer
A provider list maintained by hand
issues.objective: Make every provider-specific representation a derived adapter over the repository model, so that supporting another provider is one implementation rather than a copy of the instructions in another file.
issues.why: Provider files are the fastest-growing part of any repository that works with several assistants, and each copy drifts from the layer it was copied from. The layer is provider-neutral by design; the adapters are where a provider's requirements are allowed to exist.
issues.current_state: Provider bootstraps are generated from the registry, which is the right shape, but they land at the root and their ownership is not recorded.
issues.desired_state: Adapters are generated into the control-plane namespace, bridged at the root only where a tool truly requires a root file, and a new provider is a trait implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Every provider representation is derived from the model and declares its provenance
Adding a provider is one implementation of the adapter contract, with no edit to the layer and no new list
A provider that can be configured programmatically produces no repository file at all
Where a root file is unavoidable it is a managed bridge with recorded ownership, and its content is derived
issues.risk: An adapter layer can grow provider-shaped holes in the model beneath it. The check is whether the model would still be complete if every adapter were deleted.

issues.title: Completion comes from the command model, not from a second list
non_scope: A completion script maintained by hand
Regenerating completion on the environment-entry path if it costs more than the budget allows
issues.objective: Derive shell completion from the same command model the CLI and its documentation already come from, so that a new command is completable without anything being listed.
issues.why: A completion script is the least visible copy of a command list and therefore the one that drifts furthest. It is also the one people notice, because a missing completion reads as a missing feature.
issues.current_state: The CLI is declared once and its reference is generated. Completion, where it exists, is not derived from that declaration.
issues.desired_state: Completion is generated from the command model, refreshed as safe cached state, and never enumerated by hand.
acceptance_criteria: Completion data is derived from the command model with no second enumeration
A command added to the model is completable after the ordinary generation, with no further edit
The refresh is cached state under the control-plane namespace and never a tracked-file mutation
Whatever the entry path does for completion stays inside the entry budget
issues.risk: Completion is where a fast path tempts a shortcut list. Deriving it is cheap only if the model is already cached; otherwise the budget decides.

issues.title: This repository's own footprint moves, through the reconciler
non_scope: A broad recursive delete anywhere
Moving user-authored content without recording where it went
A shell script that performs the migration outside the reconciler
issues.objective: Migrate what this repository itself scatters — root scripts, provider files, configuration beside configuration, generated state outside the namespaces — into `.ai/` and `.majordomus/`, using the reconciler and its migrations rather than a move script.
issues.why: The tool has to survive its own contract. A repository that ships a two-folder promise while keeping a root full of exceptions is the least convincing possible demonstration, and it is also where every latent assumption about paths will surface.
issues.current_state: The footprint is what phase one recorded. Nothing has moved.
issues.desired_state: The repository conforms to its own contract, every move is recorded, and nothing that was working stopped working.
acceptance_criteria: Every move goes through a recorded migration, previewable as a dry run before it is applied
Compatibility is preserved for the paths other work depends on, or the break is deliberate, documented and migrated
After the migration this repository conforms to its own contract, checked by the same validator a foreign repository would face
Nothing that was working before stops working, proved by the full suite rather than by inspection
issues.risk: This is the phase where the tool is changed by the thing it is changing, with several sessions working in the same repository. It runs once, as a dry run first, and not concurrently with other structural work.

issues.title: The hand-maintained lists are removed, not left running beside the derivation
non_scope: Deleting a list that is genuinely authoritative for something the model does not hold
Leaving a hand-written list in place as a fallback
issues.objective: Find every list that enumerates what discovery already finds — indexes, menus, route tables, provider lists, documentation catalogues — and remove it, so that one derivation is the only one.
issues.why: Two systems doing the same job is worse than either alone: the old one keeps working just well enough that nobody notices it has diverged. This session alone found the same route list four times and a page list twice.
issues.current_state: Several such lists have been removed already; the rest are what phase one recorded and what the derivation makes redundant.
issues.desired_state: Each replaced list is deleted, its consumers read the derivation, and nothing survives as a fallback.
acceptance_criteria: The lists that are replaced are enumerated from the repository rather than assumed, and each is removed or justified as authoritative for something else
Every consumer reads the derivation after the removal, and nothing removed remains reachable as a fallback
What the interfaces show is the same as before the removal, except where the derivation is more complete
A check refuses a new enumeration of a discoverable namespace
issues.risk: A list quietly holding something the model does not carry loses that content when it goes. Each removal is checked against what the derivation actually produces, item by item.

issues.title: Every invariant of this milestone is a rule with a check that runs
non_scope: A rule with no executable check
Restating a constraint an existing rule already enforces
issues.objective: Turn the invariants — bounded footprint, no manual registration, disposable derived artifacts, reversible managed mutations, idempotent reconciliation, root files as adapters, zero-registration extension — into project rules, each with an executable check that CI runs and a negative test that proves it fires.
issues.why: Everything in this milestone decays the moment a change can land without a check noticing. A rule with no check is a suggestion, and this repository has a rule saying exactly that.
issues.current_state: The invariants exist as prose in the mission and as behaviour in the code. No rule states them and no check enforces them.
issues.desired_state: Each invariant is a rule with a check, each check has a negative test, and CI runs all of them.
acceptance_criteria: Majordomus-owned persistent state outside the two namespaces fails a check unless the ledger records it as a bridge
A secondary registry enumerating a discoverable namespace fails a check
A generated artifact without provenance, or read back as canonical input, fails a check
A mutation outside the two namespaces without a ledger entry fails a check
A non-idempotent reconciliation fails a check
Each rule has a negative test proving its check fires, and CI executes every one
issues.risk: Seven rules for one milestone is a lot of doctrine. Any constraint an existing rule already covers is referenced rather than restated, and the review has to insist on that.

issues.title: The budgets are measured, and a regression fails rather than being noticed
non_scope: A second benchmark system
A threshold so tight that ordinary content growth fails the build
issues.objective: Measure what this architecture costs — discovery, reconciliation, the environment entry, the generated artifacts — and hold each to a budget derived from its measured baseline.
issues.why: A spine every consumer reads is a cost every consumer pays. Measured once and then never again, it grows until somebody works around the tool instead of using it.
issues.current_state: The benchmark infrastructure records distributions per command against a committed baseline. The new paths are not among its targets.
issues.desired_state: Each new path is a benchmark target with a recorded baseline and a threshold that catches a material regression while tolerating ordinary growth.
acceptance_criteria: Discovery, reconciliation, the dry run and the environment entry are benchmark targets with recorded baselines
The thresholds are policy data, and the check names the target, both values and the threshold when it fails
The environment it was measured on is recorded with each baseline
A material regression fails; a byte does not
issues.risk: Wall-clock thresholds are noisy across machines. The structural counters gate strictly and the timings conservatively, as the existing performance doctrine already decided.

issues.title: A refusal says what to do about it
non_scope: A second diagnostics framework
A message that reports a condition without naming the repair
issues.objective: Make every refusal in this subsystem name the source of truth, what was observed, what was expected and the command that repairs it — through the diagnostics framework that already exists.
issues.why: The operations here refuse often by design: an edited bridge, a stale ledger, a non-conforming path, a plan that would touch something it does not own. A refusal that only says no turns a safety property into an obstacle.
issues.current_state: Errors in the executable carry structured detail in places and a bare message in others. The new operations have no convention yet.
issues.desired_state: Each refusal is actionable, and a person who has never read this code can act on it without reading this code.
acceptance_criteria: A refusal names the file or path, what was found, what was expected and the command that repairs it
An edited bridge, a ledger mismatch, a non-conforming path and a plan touching something unowned each have their own message rather than a shared generic one
The messages are exercised by tests, so a change that degrades one is caught
Machine-readable output carries the same detail as the human-readable form
issues.risk: Message quality is the first thing to decay under time pressure and the last thing anybody tests. Testing the messages is what keeps them.

issues.title: Every surface shows the integration from the one model
non_scope: A mutating integration operation exposed to unauthenticated HTTP or to a browser
A hand-edited API document, route table or documentation list
issues.objective: Project the integration state — what is adopted, what is owned, what is generated, what would change — through the CLI, the API and its document, MCP, the Cockpit and the documentation, from the one model and with no parallel definition.
issues.why: The question a person asks about an integration is what it did to my repository, and they will ask it wherever they happen to be. Answering it four ways is how the four answers begin to differ.
issues.current_state: The capability registry already projects declared operations into every surface. The integration state is not among them.
issues.desired_state: One declaration exposes the integration reads, and every surface derives from it as it does for everything else.
acceptance_criteria: The integration reads are declared once and appear in the CLI, the API, the API document, MCP, the Cockpit and the generated reference with no second registration
No mutating operation is exposed to an untrusted surface; adoption and removal stay with the trusted command line
The Cockpit shows what is adopted, what is owned and what a reconciliation would change, from that declaration
The published documentation derives its integration reference from the same model, with no retyped value
issues.risk: Showing what a reconciliation would change means running the plan on a request. Its cost belongs to the budget, and a read that builds a plan has to say so.

issues.title: A foreign repository, adopted, upgraded and given back
non_scope: A fixture the implementation recognises as a test
Declaring success from the exit code of an adoption
issues.objective: Prove the contract against a repository that is not this one: adopt it, verify the footprint, run it again, upgrade the tool, edit a bridge by hand, then remove the adoption and compare what is left against what was there before.
issues.why: Every claim in this milestone is about somebody else's repository. Proving it here, where the tool and the subject are the same tree, proves the easy half; the interesting failures are the ones this repository cannot exhibit.
issues.current_state: Nothing has been adopted anywhere but here.
issues.desired_state: One test drives the whole lifecycle on a foreign fixture and asserts each stage, including the ones designed to refuse.
acceptance_criteria: Adoption of a repository with no prior Majordomus state adds the two namespaces and the declared bridges, and nothing else, verified against the tree rather than against the report
The second adoption changes nothing
An adoption made by an older version reconciles forward without rewriting a bridge that did not need to change
A bridge edited by a person is refused rather than overwritten, and reported
Removal returns the repository to what it was, apart from authored content, compared against a recorded starting state
The fixture is ordinary in every respect and nothing in the implementation recognises it
issues.risk: An end-to-end test with a fixture the implementation special-cases proves nothing. The fixture has to be indistinguishable from a real repository.

issues.title: The milestone is accepted on its evidence
non_scope: Reporting a mechanism as proved without the artifact that proves it
issues.objective: Close the milestone: every acceptance criterion carries evidence, the measured baselines are recorded with the environment they were taken on, the adoption and removal run as documented on a clean checkout, and the remaining limitations are stated.
issues.why: A milestone is accepted by its evidence. What a later reader has is the record, not this session.
issues.current_state: Open.
issues.desired_state: Accepted with evidence against every criterion, with the footprint, the budgets and the limitations written where they will be found.
acceptance_criteria: Every acceptance criterion of the milestone has evidence recorded against it
The measured footprint of an adoption is recorded — every path, with its namespace and its owner
The budgets are recorded with the machine and environment they were measured on
The documented adoption and removal run exactly as written on a clean checkout
Pre-existing failures, failures introduced here and failures fixed here are distinguished explicitly
Remaining limitations are stated rather than omitted
issues.risk: The end of a long milestone is where intent gets recorded as outcome. Anything not demonstrated is written as a limitation.

issues.title: An identity provider is a declarative object, and Google and Facebook are two of them
non_scope: Any Rust code that reads the objects, which is I1202
A client secret, a client id or any credential value in any file of the repository
A provider-specific field that only one of the two objects can use
issues.objective: Introduce the identity-provider kind: a JSON Schema, an entry in share/kinds.yaml, the generated allow-list, a directory contract under .ai/repo/identity/providers/, and the first two objects — google and facebook — each stating its issuer, its endpoints or discovery document, the scopes it is asked for, the claim that carries a stable subject, the environment variable names its client id and client secret arrive in, its display name and its order in the sign-in offer.
issues.why: The provider set is expected to change, and the operator has said both of the first two may be struck. A provider that is a file is struck by deleting the file; a provider that is a match arm is struck by a release. Every other fact of this repository is already declared once and projected, and identity is not an exception to that.
issues.current_state: There is no identity kind, no .ai/repo/identity directory and no notion of a provider anywhere in the layer or the executable.
issues.desired_state: share/kinds.yaml carries an identity-provider kind with a schema, the allow-list is generated from that schema by majordomus generate, .ai/repo/identity/providers/ has its README chain and its two objects, and the index reports them like any other kind.
acceptance_criteria: The schema expresses one flow shape, and both objects validate against it without a per-provider escape hatch
Credentials are named, never carried: each object states the environment variable names and holds no value
The directory satisfies the recursive README and front-matter doctrine of the layer
The allow-list is generated from the schema by majordomus generate rather than written by hand
majordomus doctor reports the new kind and both objects with no diagnostic
issues.risk: A schema shaped around Google will need an escape hatch for Facebook the same day. The schema is written against the OpenID Connect flow, and any field only one provider can fill is evidence the shape is wrong.

issues.title: One typed provider model reads the objects, and no code names a provider
non_scope: The HTTP flow, which is I1203
Reading a credential value into any type that is serialised, cached, logged or rendered
issues.objective: Add apps/majordomus-cli/src/identity with the typed model of a provider object: discovery of every object under .ai/repo/identity/providers/, validation against the schema, resolution of the credential environment variables at use rather than at load, and a deterministic ordering of the sign-in offer. Expose the read as a capability so the provider list reaches the CLI, the API, OpenAPI, MCP and the Cockpit through the registry rather than through five readers.
issues.why: The objects are only canonical if exactly one thing parses them. A second reader in the Cockpit or in the HTTP layer would be a second definition of what a provider is, and would drift the first time the schema gains a field.
issues.current_state: I1201 has the objects; nothing reads them.
issues.desired_state: identity::providers() returns the validated, ordered set; a provider whose credentials are absent is reported as unavailable with a reason rather than omitted silently; and grep for the strings google and facebook in apps/ returns nothing outside tests and fixtures.
acceptance_criteria: The provider set is discovered from the directory, validated, and ordered deterministically
A provider with absent credentials is unavailable with a stated reason, and the reason reaches the surfaces
No provider identifier appears in the executable's source outside test fixtures
The read is declared once as a capability and appears in CLI, HTTP, OpenAPI, MCP and docs with no second registration
issues.risk: Resolving credentials at load makes the model unusable in any context that serialises it. They are resolved at the moment of the flow and never held.

issues.title: One flow serves every provider, and it refuses everything it did not start
non_scope: Storing anything about the reader beyond the session of I1204
A provider-specific branch anywhere in the flow
issues.objective: Implement the authorisation-code flow with PKCE once, over the typed provider model: a start route that issues state and nonce and redirects to the provider's authorisation endpoint, a callback route that refuses a state it did not issue or that has expired, exchanges the code, verifies the issuer, the audience, the expiry and the nonce of the returned identity token, and resolves the stable subject from the claim the object names.
issues.why: Two provider-specific flows are two places for a validation to be forgotten. The differences between the providers this milestone starts with are spellings of endpoints, which the objects already carry.
issues.current_state: I1202 gives the providers; there is no flow, no route and no verification.
issues.desired_state: Signing in with either declared provider works end to end against the real provider, and every refusal path — unknown state, replayed state, expired state, mismatched nonce, wrong issuer, absent credentials — is exercised by a test.
acceptance_criteria: State and nonce are single-use, expiring, and bound to the provider they were issued for
The identity token is verified for issuer, audience, expiry and nonce before any session exists
